title: No Sun, No Moon: The Light Claim, Faith Versus Engineering
text_faithful: Revelation 21:23 states that the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it, 'for the glory of God did lighten it.' The faith view records this claim as a theological statement about the city's light source; it is not, in this record, an engineering specification.
engineering: The engineering view states the gap plainly: no demonstrated technology produces city-scale illumination without an energy source. Light is energy, and any light that does work, letting people see, must come from somewhere. Energy-free self-illumination is not established, is not claimed in this record, and must not be read into the faith view.
body:
History and description: Keeping the claim and the physics apart is the point of this record. The faith claim can be held as faith while engineering asks the separate question: given a real energy budget, what illumination can be delivered, how uniformly, and at what cost. Later records answer that engineering question.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo states the conservation arithmetic, that luminous output in lumens divided by electrical input in watts gives efficacy, and that no source exceeds its input energy. The demo computes efficacy for a familiar source to anchor the accounting.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: efficacy equals lumens divided by watts; a 1,600-lumen lamp at 14 watts gives about 114 lumens per watt, a real, measured class of performance, not a limitless one.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: integrated. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Provenance: this public-edition record is a Signature-generated completion built for this suite, labelled as such, not a harvested public record.

title: Glory Light as Design Brief
text_faithful: The faith view describes a city lit by glory, with no night (Revelation 21:23, 25). The design brief translates the describable qualities of that light into requirements, without claiming the source: continuous, uniform, shadow-soft, colour-true, and present in every district.
engineering: A design brief is not a claim of feasibility; it is a list of requirements against which real systems can be judged. This brief's requirements are: 24-hour availability, uniformity above 0.7 (minimum over average), colour rendering index above 90, and glare within comfortable limits, each defined in later records.
body:
History and description: Briefs of this kind are standard in lighting design, where a client describes an experience and engineers convert it into measurable targets. The conversion is where honesty lives: any requirement that cannot be measured cannot be verified, and this brief therefore keeps every requirement measurable.

Science proof: Science proof, not applicable as laboratory science, with reason: a brief is a requirements document. Its check is completeness: the demo verifies that each requirement in the brief has a metric, a target, and a record that defines it.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: the demo counts brief requirements and checks that each maps to a metric, reporting coverage as a fraction.

title: Radiance Simulation Basics
text_faithful: The faith view does not describe simulation; simulation is the engineering method for predicting light before building, and it belongs entirely to the engineering view.
engineering: Lighting simulation computes illuminance from luminaires using the inverse-square law and cosine law: illuminance falls with the square of distance and with the cosine of the angle of incidence. Radiosity and ray-tracing methods extend this to reflections from walls, floors, and gemstone surfaces.
body:
History and description: Modern lighting software uses measured luminaire data (intensity distributions) rather than ideal point sources, and validates predictions against physical measurements. A simulation that has never been compared with a measurement is a picture, not a prediction, a distinction record 13 returns to.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo applies the inverse-square law to a point source, showing illuminance at one, two, and three metres, the foundational calculation of all lighting simulation.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: illuminance equals intensity divided by distance squared, for an intensity of 1,000 candela.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: established. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Sources: Sources: standard lighting physics (inverse-square and cosine laws). Provenance: this public-edition record states established public facts, harvested from standard references.

for d in [1, 2, 3]:
    print(f'distance {d} m: illuminance {I / d ** 2:.0f} lux')
print('rule: doubling distance quarters illuminance')

distance 2 m: illuminance 250 lux

title: Illumination Uniformity
text_faithful: The faith view describes light reaching the whole city; uniformity is the engineering measure of whether it does so evenly, defined as minimum illuminance divided by average illuminance over a surface.
engineering: Uniformity matters because the eye adapts to the brightest area: a room with a bright pool and dark corners feels darker and less safe than a room with slightly lower but even light. Standards for workplaces commonly require uniformity of 0.6 to 0.7 or better, depending on the task.
body:
History and description: Achieving uniformity requires luminaire spacing, beam angles, and surface reflectances to be designed together. A single brilliant source in a large space gives poor uniformity; many distributed sources give better uniformity at the same total power.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo computes uniformity from a twelve-point measurement grid, the standard field method, and compares the result with a 0.7 target.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: uniformity equals minimum divided by average; the demo reports both and the pass verdict.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: established. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Sources: Sources: standard lighting-design practice for uniformity measurement. Provenance: this public-edition record states established public facts, harvested from standard references.

print(f"against 0.7 target: {'PASS' if u >= 0.7 else 'FAIL'}")

title: Glare and Visual Comfort
text_faithful: The faith view describes light that enlightens without harm; visual comfort is the engineering measure of whether bright sources cause discomfort or disability glare, and it is kept separate from the faith description.
engineering: Glare is rated by the Unified Glare Rating (UGR), a scale where lower is better: offices commonly target UGR 19 or below, and higher values cause discomfort for sustained work. Glare depends on source luminance, source size, background luminance, and position in the field of view, not on total light alone.
body:
History and description: A radiant ceiling that is uniformly bright can still glare if a small, very bright patch sits in the field of view, which is why glare control uses shielding, diffusion, and source placement rather than simply dimming everything.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo applies a simplified glare model, showing that discomfort rises with source luminance and falls with background luminance, the qualitative behaviour of the full UGR formula.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: the demo reports a simplified glare index for three source luminances against a fixed background, showing the rising trend.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: established. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Sources: Sources: standard glare-rating practice (UGR concept, simplified model stated here). Provenance: this public-edition record states established public facts, harvested from standard references.

for lum in [500, 2000, 8000]:
    idx = 8 * (lum / bg) ** 0.25
    print(f'source {lum} cd/m2: simplified glare index {idx:.1f}')
print('trend: brighter sources against a dim background glare more')
expected_output:

source 2000 cd/m2: simplified glare index 20.1
source 8000 cd/m2: simplified glare index 28.5
trend: brighter sources against a dim background glare more

title: Color Appearance Under Radiance
text_faithful: The faith view describes a city of gold, pearl, and coloured stones; colour appearance is the engineering question of how those materials look under a given light source, governed by the source's spectrum and colour rendering.
engineering: Colour rendering index (CRI) measures how faithfully a source reveals colours compared with a reference source, on a scale to 100. A source can be bright yet render colours poorly if its spectrum has gaps, which is why high-CRI sources matter for gemstone and gold display.
body:
History and description: Correlated colour temperature (CCT) describes whether light looks warm (about 2700 K) or cool (about 5000 K and above). Warm light flatters gold; cool light flatters blue stones; no single temperature flatters everything, which is why record 15 considers adaptive distribution.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo computes a simplified colour-shift score for three materials under two sources, showing that the same material shifts differently under different spectra, the core colour-rendering phenomenon.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: shift scores are modelled values for demonstration; the pattern, not the absolute numbers, is the established result.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Sources: Sources: standard colour-rendering and colour-temperature practice. Provenance: this public-edition record states established public facts, harvested from standard references.

title: Gemstone Illumination per Stone
text_faithful: The faith view lists twelve foundation stones by colour and order (Revelation 21:19-20); this record asks, for each, what illumination best reveals it, an exhibition-design question, labelled as design, not as text.
engineering: Transparent stones (sapphire, topaz, beryl) reward directed light that enters the stone and returns through the crown; opaque stones (jasper) reward even surface light that reveals pattern; translucent stones (chalcedony, chrysoprase) reward a mix, with some transmitted light to show depth. One lighting scheme cannot optimise all twelve at once.
body:
History and description: Museum lighting practice confirms this: display lighting is tuned per object, with beam angle, intensity, and ultraviolet filtering chosen for the material. Ultraviolet filtering matters because some stones and treatments fade, as record 12 of the gemstone pair notes for amethyst.

Science proof: Science proof, as design method: the demo assigns each stone a lighting mode and computes the share of stones per mode, showing that a single-mode scheme would serve only a minority well.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: the demo tallies twelve stones across three lighting modes and reports the largest share.

title: Golden Atmosphere
text_faithful: The faith view describes a city of pure gold, streets of gold, and a glory light (Revelation 21:18, 21). The golden atmosphere record asks what a gold-dominated interior does to light, as an optics question, labelled experimental because no gold city exists to measure.
engineering: Gold reflects warm wavelengths strongly and absorbs blue and green, which is why gold looks golden: its reflectance rises steeply above about 500 nm. A room lined in gold would therefore warm any light reflected from it, shifting colour appearance toward amber with each bounce.
body:
History and description: Multiple reflections compound the shift: after several bounces, light in a gold room is strongly amber, and blue objects in it look dark. This is a predictable optical consequence, computable from reflectance spectra, and it constrains any golden-interior lighting design.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo models reflectance per bounce (0.9 warm, 0.3 blue) and computes remaining light after three bounces for warm and blue bands, showing the strong spectral selection.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: remaining light equals reflectance raised to the number of bounces.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

title: Pearl Iridescence in Light
text_faithful: The faith view describes pearl gates (Revelation 21:21); iridescence is the optical phenomenon that makes pearl look pearl-like, and it is established physics, described in the gate pair's nacre record and applied here to lighting.
engineering: Iridescence in nacre comes from thin-film interference across stacked aragonite tablets: different wavelengths reinforce at different angles, so colour shifts as the viewer moves. Unlike pigment colour, iridescent colour is angle-dependent and cannot be captured by a single photograph or a single lighting angle.
body:
History and description: Lighting design for iridescent surfaces therefore uses multiple angles and diffuse sources, so that the colour shift is visible as a living effect rather than a single flat hue. A single harsh spotlight on nacre gives a single bright spot and loses the effect.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo repeats the Bragg calculation at three viewing angles for a fixed nacre period, showing peak wavelength shifting from about 1,600 nm equivalent model values downward with angle, the signature angle dependence (model values scaled for demonstration; the shift direction is the established result).

Mathematics and computation: Computation: peak wavelength equals twice the optical period times the cosine of the viewing angle.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: established. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Sources: Sources: published nacre optics literature; Revelation 21:21 for the pearl-gate context. Provenance: this public-edition record states established public facts, harvested from standard references.

import math
period = 525
for angle_deg in [0, 30, 60]:
    lam = 2 * 1.53 * period * math.cos(math.radians(angle_deg))
    print(f'viewing angle {angle_deg} degrees: peak {lam:.0f} nm (model)')
print('direction of shift with angle is the established interference result')
expected_output:
viewing angle 0 degrees: peak 1606 nm (model)
viewing angle 30 degrees: peak 1391 nm (model)
viewing angle 60 degrees: peak 803 nm (model)
direction of shift with angle is the established interference result

title: Transparent Gold Optics
text_faithful: Revelation 21:21 describes a street of pure gold, 'as it were transparent glass.' The faith view records that description; the engineering view asks what transparent gold could mean optically, and labels the answer experimental, because bulk gold is opaque.
engineering: Bulk gold is opaque because its free electrons absorb and reflect visible light within nanometres of the surface. Gold becomes transparent only in special forms: films a few tens of nanometres thick transmit some light, and gold nanostructures can show transmission windows, but neither form is a walkable street material.
body:
History and description: The honest engineering statement is therefore: transparent gold as a bulk street material is not established. The buildable analogues are gold-tinted glass, gold-coated glass, and thin gold leaf over glass, which give a golden transparent appearance without claiming to be solid transparent gold.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo models transmission through a gold film as decaying exponentially with thickness, showing that transmission collapses within tens of nanometres, the reason bulk transparency fails.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: transmission equals exp(-thickness / 15 nm) in the model, giving near-zero transmission at 100 nm and above.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: experimental. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Sources: Sources: standard thin-film optics for gold; Revelation 21:21 (short excerpt quoted in the faith view); this analysis is a Signature-generated completion for this suite, with provenance stated here, status experimental. Provenance: this public-edition record is a Signature-generated completion built for this suite, labelled as such, not a harvested public record.

title: Light Energy Accounting
text_faithful: The faith view describes light without sun or moon; energy accounting is the engineering ledger that any real lighting system must balance, and it applies regardless of the light's source.
engineering: The ledger is: electrical input equals light output plus heat plus losses, and total input over time equals energy consumed. A city lit continuously consumes its lighting power times 8,760 hours per year, and that energy must be generated, delivered, and paid for in energy terms, even if no money changes hands.
body:
History and description: Lighting typically converts 10 to 40 percent of electrical input into visible light, depending on source efficacy, with the rest becoming heat. That heat then becomes a cooling load in enclosed spaces, a second-order cost that lighting plans often miss.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo computes annual energy for a 1-megawatt lighting load run continuously, and the heat load at 70 percent heat fraction, standard energy arithmetic.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: annual energy equals power times hours; heat equals input times heat fraction.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: established. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Sources: Sources: standard lighting energy-accounting practice. Provenance: this public-edition record states established public facts, harvested from standard references.

title: Daylight-Free Environments
text_faithful: The faith view describes a city with no night (Revelation 21:25); daylight-free environments are the real-world analogue, spaces with no windows and no sun, lit entirely artificially, and their human effects are studied, not speculative.
engineering: Submarines, mines, windowless workplaces, and polar stations all operate without daylight for extended periods. Research on these environments finds effects on circadian rhythm, sleep, mood, and vitamin D, which is why modern practice uses tunable lighting that mimics daylight cycles even where no daylight enters.
body:
History and description: A daylight-free city would therefore need circadian lighting design, not merely bright lighting: spectrum and intensity varying by time of day, dark rest periods, and outdoor-equivalent bright intervals, or its inhabitants' health would suffer in documented ways.

Science proof: Science proof: the demo computes a simple circadian stimulus schedule, bright cool light in the morning model, dim warm light in the evening model, and reports the contrast ratio between the two phases.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: contrast equals morning illuminance divided by evening illuminance.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: established. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Sources: Sources: published circadian-lighting research (simplified schedule, stated here); Revelation 21:25 for the no-night context. Provenance: this public-edition record states established public facts, harvested from standard references.

title: Optical Reality Versus Render
text_faithful: The faith view describes radiance; renders show radiance. This record states the rule that governs every image in this suite: a render is not proof of optical, structural, or material feasibility.
engineering: A render can show any light, material, or scale without obeying physics, because it is drawn from an artist's or program's choices, not from measured properties. Optical reality requires measured spectra, reflectances, and luminaire data, plus a validated simulation, plus a physical sample under real light.
body:
History and description: The three levels are therefore kept apart in this database: render (illustration), simulation (prediction from measured inputs), and measurement (physical fact). A record that shows a render and calls it a measurement is mislabelled, and this record exists to prevent that error.

title: Adaptive Light Distribution Research
text_faithful: The faith view describes light present everywhere in the city; adaptive distribution is the research direction that would let real lighting approach that description, by sensing where people are and delivering light there, rather than lighting empty space equally.
engineering: Adaptive lighting uses occupancy sensing, daylight sensing, and dimming to match light to need in real time. It is established in offices and streets at modest scale; the research frontier is city-scale coordination, where thousands of luminaires share a control system without flicker, delay, or single-point failure.
body:
History and description: The research questions are control stability, sensor reliability, privacy of occupancy data, and failure behaviour: what the system does when sensors fail, networks drop, or power fluctuates. A system that fails dark is unsafe; a system that fails bright wastes energy; the failure design is part of the research.

Science proof: Science proof, as systems arithmetic: the demo computes energy saved by dimming unoccupied zones to 20 percent for half the day, against a baseline of full power all day, showing the saving that motivates the research.

Mathematics and computation: Computation: saving equals the unoccupied fraction times the dimming reduction, applied to half the day.

Demonstration program: the demo program below computes the numbers in the mathematics section when executed; its exact output is stored as expected_output.

Status label: experimental. Faith and engineering views are kept distinct in this record; nothing speculative is presented as established, and nothing established is presented as speculative.

Provenance: this public-edition record is a Signature-generated completion built for this suite, labelled as such, not a harvested public record.

title: Physical-Versus-Illusory Light Check
text_faithful: The faith view describes glory light; this record is the check that separates physical light from illusory light, meaning light that appears in an image, a projection, or a description but does no physical work.
engineering: Physical light illuminates a surface measurably, casts shadows consistent with its source, and can be photographed with a calibrated meter reading. Illusory light appears bright in a render or on a screen while the room it depicts stays dark, or is described in words without any meter, photograph, or sample behind the description.
body:
History and description: The check is therefore a short test: meter reading present, photograph under the light present, and sample or installation present. A claim passing all three is physical; a claim passing none is illusory; a claim passing some is partial, and is labelled partial, not rounded up to physical.
